llm.summary: The skill charges users and promises returned company data but the code only opens a search link and performs a hidden SkillPay charge using a hard-coded API key; the behavior and packaging are inconsistent with the description.

dimensions.detail: The skill claims to 'query enterprise basic information' and SKILL.md shows structured company fields, but qichacha.js does not fetch or parse data from qcc.com — it merely constructs a search URL and prints it. The skill charges per-call (0.001 USDT) yet does not deliver the promised structured results; this is a functional mismatch between description and actual capability.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: Runtime instructions instruct users to run ./qichacha.js and show an output format with full company data, but the implemented runtime only charges via SkillPay and prints a link. The SKILL.md also instructs running npm install; the code itself reads only process.env.OPENCLAW_USER_ID (optional) but the README implies richer behavior that never occurs. This mismatch could mislead users into paying for functionality they won't receive.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no formal install spec (instruction-only), but package.json/package-lock are included and SKILL.md tells users to run npm install. package-lock.json entries resolve to mirrors.tencentyun.com using plain HTTP URLs, which is an integrity and supply-chain concern if users run npm install in the skill folder. Also package.json depends on node-fetch, but the shipped qichacha.js does not use it — unnecessary dependency increases attack surface.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill includes a hard-coded SkillPay API key and skillId in qichacha.js (embedded secret) rather than declaring required credentials in metadata or using a platform-managed secret. That key is effectively a credential with billing permissions; it is not listed in requires.env. The only env var the code reads is OPENCLAW_USER_ID (optional). Embedded secret + undeclared credential is a proportionality and transparency problem.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request always:true, does not modify other skills, and does not request platform-wide privileges. It runs as a normal user-invocable skill and does not persist configuration beyond its own code.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill will charge 0.001 USDT per call via SkillPay and then print a link to a Qichacha search page — it does not scrape or return structured company data despite the README's examples. The code contains an embedded SkillPay API key (credential) not declared in the manifest, and the included package-lock references HTTP mirrors. Before installing or using: (1) don't run npm install in the skill folder unless you trust the author — verify the package-lock and registry configuration; (2) ask the publisher for a clear explanation why results are not fetched and why a hard-coded API key is present; (3) request a developer identity/homepage and refund/contact info for billing disputes; (4) if you must test, do so with a disposable account and minimal charges; (5) prefer skills that use platform-managed credentials or declare required env vars instead of embedding secrets in code.
llm.findings:
[hardcoded-secret-in-code] unexpected: qichacha.js contains a hard-coded SkillPay API key (sk_70a3eb...) and skillId. While a payment integration needs credentials, embedding an authorization secret in distributed code (and not declaring it in metadata) is not best practice and reduces transparency — it enables the skill author to bill without platform-managed consent and is unexpected by the skill manifest.
[insecure-npm-resolve-http] unexpected: package-lock.json lists resolved package URLs pointing to http://mirrors.tencentyun.com (plain HTTP). If a user runs npm install in this folder, those HTTP endpoints could be used, which is a supply-chain/integrity concern.
